flawed_step: The step from edge-transitivity (plus regularity) to vertex-transitivity cannot be justified. Transitivity on unordered edges does not give an automorphism that swaps the two ends of an edge. Bipartite semisymmetric graphs have two vertex classes that no automorphism exchanges.
counterexample: Folkman graph. Vertices: the 10 two-element subsets {a,b} of {1..5} (type E), and the 10 vertices x_1, x_2 for x in {1..5} (type C). Edges: {a,b} is joined to a_1, a_2, b_1, b_2, giving 40 edges. 4-regular: each {a,b} has 4 neighbours; each x_i lies in the 4 subsets containing x. Edge-transitive: every permutation s of {1..5} acts by {a,b}->{s(a),s(b)}, x_i->s(x)_i, and swapping x_1<->x_2 is an automorphism since they have the same neighbours. The edge ({a,b},a_i) goes to ({c,d},c_j) by taking s with a->c, b->d, then swapping c_1,c_2 if i!=j. Not vertex-transitive: 1_1 and 1_2 have the same neighbourhood {{1,2},{1,3},{1,4},{1,5}}, so 1_1 has a twin. {1,2} has no twin: a twin would need neighbourhood {1_1,1_2,2_1,2_2}, but type-C vertices have only type-E neighbours, and a different subset {c,d} has neighbourhood {c_1,c_2,d_1,d_2}. Automorphisms preserve having a twin, so none maps 1_1 to {1,2}.
assessment_summary: False. The Folkman graph (20 vertices, 4-regular) is edge-transitive but not vertex-transitive. Edge-transitivity comes from S5 permutations plus swapping the paired vertices x_1, x_2. Vertex-transitivity fails because vertices x_i have a twin (a vertex with the same neighbours) while subset vertices {a,b} do not.
